newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Asian robustas gain ground in UK.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Asian robustas gain ground in UK.

text.p: British robusta coffee imports are increasingly being met by Asian origins at the expense of African sources, the head of the UK Coffee Federation said. In an interview, Anthony Miller, executive chairman of the federation, also doubted if there would be a big uplift in coffee prices next year unless there is a crop disaster.
And he said the UK, principally a consumer of the arabica coffee variety, is unlikely significantly to switch to robustas.
On prices, he said the market, as in 1996, could see a reasonable degree of stability next year.
"Unless there is a disaster then surely with more coffee becoming 'technically' available there seems little chance of a major uplift in world prices," he said.
Coffee saw a turbulent period in 1994 when frosts and drought hit Brazil, pushing robusta prices to near 10-year highs of $4,140 a tonne. They are now around $1,430 a tonne.
Miller said the arabica, regarded as better quality to robusta, forms 60 percent of UK's imports of about 1.85 million 60-kg bags in 1996 and the remaining 40 percent is robusta.

"As for the future, we would not expect the 60/40 split to vary greatly," he said. Miller said Indonesian, Vietnamese and Thai coffee form some 32 percent of UK coffee imports in 1996, up from about 22 percent in 1995.

"The gains within the robusta sector made by these three countries were at the expense of African robusta coffee imports which have, over the years, fallen back from their earlier commanding position," he said.

He gave no reasons for the growing tide of Asian robustas but stressed that origins that would succeed with imports into the UK are "those that pay much care and attention to quality issues..." Miller said some leading UK coffee firms had set up shop in the former Eastern Bloc countries in anticipation of a strong consumption growth.
"The amount of consumer activity in this field has to date been rather less than was at first anticipated," he said.

This was largely due to a relatively low level of disposal income. But he expects the situation to correct itself in time. On the speciality coffee sector, Miller said his members readily recognised the growth potential in the sector.
"The continued growth in travel makes consumers more aware of products enjoyed in other markets which in turn leads an enhanced interest back home," he said.
Miller said UK roasting capacity is viewed as being adequate to meet foreseeable demand.
"As in all areas of activity such matters are kept under careful and constant review," he said. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
